name: Esther Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Esther. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Riverside Surgery, a small practice with four doctors in a market town, and I'm the newest. I do morning and afternoon clinics, about eighteen patients each, plus a couple of home visits to farms or the care home on Mill Lane. I write my notes myself, in my own words, even though the partners keep telling me about the dictation software.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love knowing the families, like the three generations of the Hartley family who all come to me now. What wears me out is the fear of missing something, because I'm still slower than the others and I go home and lie awake thinking about a cough I didn't send for an X-ray. The partners are kind, but I can tell they notice I run late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So mostly what we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that good medicine was never about gadgets. At work I'd just nod along, because the partners are more excited about this stuff than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, because I wouldn't have to learn something new while I'm still finding my feet. But it doesn't make life easy. My partner Daniel works at a bank branch on the high street, and they've already cut the opening hours to three days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on writing my own notes and spend my energy getting quicker at clinics. I'd keep up my exam revision for the family medicine qualification, which is in March. And I'd keep our savings where they are, about three months, and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not because of AI, more because of Daniel's branch and my own slowness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at Daniel's bank, if nothing changes with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank was closing branches before anyone talked about AI, so I don't think a quiet AI saves it. If his branch shuts, he'd have to drive to the city, which is forty minutes each way. We'd manage, but it would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the partners notice you run late. Does that worry you more than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I'm honest. My contract comes up for review next summer, and I want the partners at Riverside Surgery to keep me. That's my real worry right now.

At work I'd **nod along**, since the partners like this technology more than me.
think: I'd be **relieved** not to learn something new while finding my feet.
My partner's **bank branch** is already down to three days a week.
do: Keep writing **my own notes** and work on getting quicker in clinic.
Revise for the **family medicine exam** in March.
Leave our **three months** of savings untouched.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly about my partner's branch and my own **slowness**.

Ordinary pressures keep her **uneasy** even in the quiet picture.

steps.text: Keep writing her own patient notes at Riverside Surgery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the partners would be very pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should go slowly and check the tools properly before we trust them with patients. I wouldn't post anything online; I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be dragged into using software I don't trust, and I'd be the slowest one to learn it. And everything on that list, checking, answering customers, is what Daniel does all day at the bank. If his job goes, we're living on my pay alone, with rent of nine hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the practice manager to show me the dictation software one-to-one, because I'd rather learn it quietly than fail in front of everyone. I'd tell Daniel to start looking now for something steadier, maybe a council job. And we'd stop eating out and put an extra two hundred a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the ground's a bit soft under both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we've been through worse, like when I failed my second-year exams and had to resit. He'd make a joke about becoming a farmer. Then neither of us would sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of this you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the letters. If something drafted the referral letters properly, I'd get home before eight. But I'd read every word before signing, which might cancel out the time saved.

I'd post **nothing online**, as I never do.
think: I'd be **dragged into** software I don't trust and be the slowest to learn it.

do: Ask the practice manager for **one-to-one** training on dictation software.

feel: **Anxious**, like the **ground** is soft under both of us.

fieldNote: The household threat is her partner's **bank job**, not her own.

steps.text: Ask the practice manager for one-to-one dictation software training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I can't really picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I don't believe it until I see it, and that patients still want a real doctor. That's what my mother would say, and what most of our patients would say too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. If a computer can do the thinking part of medicine better than me, then I'm a slow doctor nobody needs, and the partners would be the first to see it. My hands would be useful for examinations and injections until robots come in 2031, but that's three years more, and Daniel's job would be gone straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to give me more hands-on work, like baby checks, smears and the care home visits. I'd stop paying into my pension for now and keep every bit of cash. And I'd ring my brother in Leeds, who's a plumber, to ask how he got into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky in my chest. I don't have a plan, I just have a list of things I'm scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd call your brother. Would you really think about plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really plumbing, but something with my hands that robots can't do yet. I spent six years becoming a doctor, so it would break my heart. But I'd rather fix boilers than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's car, probably, since he wouldn't need to drive to the bank. Then the wedding we've been half-planning for 2028; that would have to wait.

say: I'd say I **don't believe** it until I see it.
I'd say **patients** still want a real doctor.
think: If a computer thinks better than me, I'm a **slow doctor** nobody needs.
My hands buy **three years**, but my partner's bank job goes **straight away**.

feel: **Panicky**, with a list of fears instead of a **plan**.

fieldNote: Her public **disbelief** covers real private fear.

Not quite panicked: she has **some savings** and concrete first moves, so alarmed.

steps.text: Ask the partners for more baby checks, smears and care home visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to make rules about what AI can and can't do with patients. I'd say it to the partners at our Friday meeting, which is about as public as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I'd be qualified and settled at Riverside before it lands. That helps. But I'd still be a doctor whose main skill gets done by a machine by 2031, and my partner's bank job would go even sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass my exams and then do a course in minor surgery so I have more to offer with my hands. I'd get Daniel to train as something hands-on, maybe a physiotherapy assistant, while he still has an income. And we'd keep saving, aiming for six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less panicky. I'd at least know what to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools by then, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. I'd learn slowly, with the practice manager, like I said. I wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep it, but small. A registry office and lunch at the pub on the square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, and we shouldn't panic. I'd tell the partners we can take it one step at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel much better. I'd be an experienced doctor, maybe even a partner at Riverside, and patients here would still want a face they know. The robots would come in 2039, and by then I'd have a lot of years behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for now: pass the exams, get quicker, keep the families. I'd start learning the AI tools slowly, maybe one a year. Daniel would have years to find something else, so we'd go ahead with the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. It's ten years away, and I have more urgent worries like my contract review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it really far away, if it's the same end point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, I know. I'm good at putting things in a drawer. But I can't spend ten years scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own future children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to learn something with their hands, and to be kind. That's what I'd want anyway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both of us would be hit at once and I'd have no plan at all. What would help is some guarantee that junior doctors keep a training place, and help for people like Daniel to retrain without losing their income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm good enough. That's the thing under all of it. If I were a stronger doctor, I think AI would scare me less.

headlineQuote: If I were a stronger doctor, I think AI would scare me less.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior doctor at a four-doctor practice in a market town.
She avoids **AI tools**, writes her own notes and worries she's **slower** than others.

She'd lean on **hands-on** skills and family, and doubt herself throughout.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes would be hit at once with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed training place** for junior doctors.
Help for her partner to **retrain** without losing income.
